rationale: Both give a credible literature summary, covering embedding and LM-head sensitivity, first and last blocks, down and output projections, and outlier-driven sensitivity (LLM.int8, AWQ). Both then propose a similar label-free procedure: unlabelled calibration text, per-layer proxy scores including single-layer quantize-and-measure KL, a top-k allocation to 8-bit with structural protections, and held-out validation via perplexity, logit KL, CKA and qualitative checks. A's strengths are that it includes the principled Hessian/Fisher-trace signal (HAWQ-style), which B omits, and adds an allocation-versus-perplexity knee sweep. Its weaknesses are a bit-budget formula that claims parameter weighting but ignores it, and a few loose literature attributions. B's strengths are keeping normalization parameters at higher precision and an AWQ-style salient-channel step for the 4-bit layers. It states the key assumption that distribution shift stands in for task quality, along with when that fails, and it adds a strong negative-control validation that swaps the allocation to show the ranking carries information. B's weaknesses are a confused claim that 8-bit layers will show lower CKA and some unit sloppiness. The strengths and flaws balance out.
